content.text:
J'ai regardé le fichier, et ce que je t'ai dit hier (« seam nécessaire, comme pour docker ») passe à côté du vrai sujet. Il y a un bug de fond.

## Le bug : l'isolation par contexte ne marche pas

Les trois méthodes encodent le contexte DevDesk dans le champ `path` du protocole credential de git :

```
protocol=https
host=gitlab.com
path=devdesk/context/prod     ← censé isoler les contextes
username=oauth2
password=<token>
```

Or git **ignore le `path` par défaut** : `credential.useHttpPath` vaut `false`, et git strippe le chemin avant de transmettre au helper. Vérifié à l'instant avec un store jetable :

```
approve  path=devdesk/context/default  password=TOKEN_DEFAULT
approve  path=devdesk/context/prod     password=TOKEN_PROD

$ cat creds
REDACTED     ← une seule entrée

$ git credential fill  (path=devdesk/context/default)
password=TOKEN_PROD                               ← le mauvais token
```

Conséquence concrète : deux contextes DevDesk pointant sur le même hôte GitLab **s'écrasent mutuellement**. Après `:context prod`, le contexte `default` renvoie le token de `prod`. Le stockage est en réalité clé par `protocol://host`, pas par contexte — et ça échoue silencieusement, sans erreur.

Ça touche tous les helpers (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), pas seulement `store` : le strip a lieu dans git lui-même, avant le helper.

Avec `useHttpPath = true`, ça marche comme prévu — deux entrées distinctes, bon token renvoyé. Mais c'est une config globale de l'utilisateur, que DevDesk ne pose nulle part et qui modifierait le comportement de git pour tous ses autres dépôts. Le vrai correctif est probablement d'encoder le contexte dans le `host` (`gitlab.com` → clé dérivée) ou dans le `username`, plutôt que dans un champ que git est libre de jeter.

## Défauts secondaires

- **`Delete` n'a pas de timeout** (`git_credential.go:160`) alors que `Save` et `Load` en ont un de 2 s. Le commentaire de `Save` explique pourquoi il est là : éviter que le TUI se fige si GCM n'est pas configuré ou attend une saisie. Le logout n'a pas cette protection.
- **Le timeout ne tue pas ce qu'il annonce.** Le commentaire dit « tuer le processus et tous ses enfants », mais `cmd.Process.Kill()` ne tue que le fils direct. GCM spawn un sous-processus qui survit.
- **`HelperStorage` (`helper.go`, 137 lignes) est du code mort** : construit nulle part hors de son propre fichier et d'un test. C'est `GitCredentialStorage` qui est câblé dans `internal/app/app.go`. Et il est buggé — `detectHelper()` peut renvoyer `store --file=/path`, que `"credential-"+helper` transforme en un seul argv `credential-store --file=/path`, introuvable. Il code aussi `protocol=https` en dur là où `GitCredentialStorage` parse le scheme.

## Ce que ça change pour les tests

La testabilité est en fait **moins** problématique que pour docker. Pas besoin de seam : `git credential` est entièrement pilotable par l'environnement.

```go
t.Setenv("GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL", filepath.Join(dir, "gitconfig"))  // helper = store --file=<tmp>
t.Setenv("GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM", "1")
```

C'est ce que je viens de faire à la main : hermétique, rapide, et ça ne touche pas le trousseau réel de l'utilisateur — ce qui serait inacceptable pour un test. On teste le vrai binaire git plutôt qu'un stub, donc on attrape des bugs comme celui du `path`, qu'un stub aurait au contraire figé dans le marbre.

Un seam resterait utile pour un seul cas : simuler le timeout sans attendre 2 s.

**Donc l'ordre logique s'inverse.** Écrire les tests d'abord graverait le comportement cassé. Je propose : corriger l'isolation de contexte, supprimer `helper.go`, puis couvrir. Tu veux que je parte là-dessus, ou que je consigne d'abord ces défauts dans le backlog pour que tu tranches sur la stratégie de clé ?

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

D1, D3 and D6 — the byte-vs-rune lot — were fixed together; see
[§1.1](#11-fixed). The remainder is unfixed and reachable from the current code.

### D2 — The "permanent delete" checkbox is documented as locked but is not

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:35` and `:99-105`

`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent` pre-checks *Immediate deletion* and its doc
comment states the box is non-modifiable ("pré-cochée et non modifiable"). Nothing
enforces that: `space` and `enter` on the checkbox still toggle it.

A project already marked for deletion can therefore be sent through a
grace-period delete that the caller does not expect. Pinned by
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable`.

**Fix:** carry a `locked` flag on the modal and make the toggle a no-op when set,
or drop the claim from the doc comment.

### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`

`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.

Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
than a drive-by fix.

### D5 — Unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`

`internal/ui/components/creation_form.go:221-223`

After cycling the resource type, the code clamps `focusedField` down to
`maxField()`. The surrounding branch only runs when `focusedField == 0`, and
`maxField()` is never below 4, so the clamp can never fire.

Dead defensive code. Harmless, but it implies a state transition that cannot
happen and is misleading to read.

### D7 — `extractTarGz` keeps parent references in archive paths

`internal/oci/oci.go:262`

Extraction strips leading `./` and `/` but does not reject `..`, so an archive
member named `../../etc/passwd` survives as a map key containing parent
references.

**Not exploitable today.** The sole consumer, `applyTemplate` in

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

D1, D3 and D6 — the byte-vs-rune lot — were fixed together; see
[§1.1](#11-fixed). The remainder is unfixed and reachable from the current code.

### D2 — The "permanent delete" checkbox is documented as locked but is not

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:35` and `:99-105`

`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent` pre-checks *Immediate deletion* and its doc
comment states the box is non-modifiable ("pré-cochée et non modifiable"). Nothing
enforces that: `space` and `enter` on the checkbox still toggle it.

A project already marked for deletion can therefore be sent through a
grace-period delete that the caller does not expect. Pinned by
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable`.

**Fix:** carry a `locked` flag on the modal and make the toggle a no-op when set,
or drop the claim from the doc comment.

### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`

`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.

Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
than a drive-by fix.

### D5 — Unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`

`internal/ui/components/creation_form.go:221-223`

After cycling the resource type, the code clamps `focusedField` down to
`maxField()`. The surrounding branch only runs when `focusedField == 0`, and
`maxField()` is never below 4, so the clamp can never fire.

Dead defensive code. Harmless, but it implies a state transition that cannot
happen and is misleading to read.

### D7 — `extractTarGz` keeps parent references in archive paths

`internal/oci/oci.go:262`

Extraction strips leading `./` and `/` but does not reject `..`, so an archive
member named `../../etc/passwd` survives as a map key containing parent
references.

**Not exploitable today.** The sole consumer, `applyTemplate` in
`internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go:1053`, turns the map into GitLab commit
actions rather than writing to disk, and the server validates the paths.

Recorded because the hazard is latent: any future caller that writes these keys
under a target directory inherits a Zip Slip. Pinned by
`TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys`.

**Fix:** reject entries whose cleaned path escapes the root, before returning
them.

### 1.1 Fixed

**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.

Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
ones.

A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
gone.

The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).

One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.

---

## 2. Technical debt

### Test coverage

Currently **18.2 %** overall; the agreed target is 80 %, which needs roughly
**+7 250 covered statements** over today's ~2 100.

Phased plan, with the harness and most of phase 1 delivered:

| Phase | Scope | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `internal/ui/testutil` Bubble Tea harness | **done** (100 %) |
| 1 | Leaf components and pure helpers | **done** except the `ui/theme` complement (~55 stmts) |
| 2 | Mid-size view state machines (`status`, `containers`, `dashboard`, `gitlab/auth`) | pending (~1 240 stmts) |
| 3 | Large views (`workspaces`, `explorer`, `security`, `netdiag`) | pending (~2 470 stmts) |
| 4 | `ui/oci_resources` | pending (~1 995 stmts) |
| 5 | Router and I/O seams (`app`, `scan`, `docker`) | pending (~1 360 stmts) |
| 6 | Remainder to reach 80 % | pending (~400 stmts) |

Phase 1 progress:

| Package | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/ui/testutil` | — | **100 %** (new) |
| `internal/ui/shortcut` | 0 % | **100 %** |
| `internal/ui/help` | 0 % | **96.7 %** |
| `internal/ui/components` | 0 % | **79.8 %** |
| `internal/oci` | 0 % | **33.6 %** |
| `internal/docker` | 7.3 % | **65.4 %** (phase 5, pulled forward — see below) |
| `internal/gitlab` | 7.5 % | **100 %** |
| `internal/credentials` | 29.5 % | **98.2 %** |

`internal/oci` stops at 33.6 % because the remaining statements are registry HTTP
paths (`DownloadTemplate`, `listCatalog`, `ListTemplates`) that need a fuller
`httptest` fixture — a manifest plus a gzipped layer — rather than the
single-response stubs used so far.

Phase 5's blocker is cleared for `docker`: the package now routes every CLI
invocation through the `dockerRunner` seam in `internal/docker/exec.go`, so tests
drive argument building and output parsing against canned output. `scan` and
`app` remain.

`internal/gitlab` needed no seam: every function takes a `*gitlabclient.Client`
built from a base URL, so an `httptest` server standing in for the API covers
the whole package. `Clone` is exercised against a throwaway local repository
rather than mocked, and skips when no `git` binary is on `PATH`.

### Files over the 800-line ceiling

The project's own coding rules cap files at 800 lines. Seven exceed it:

| File | Lines |
|---|---|
| `internal/ui/security/model.go` | 1785 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/update.go` | 1556 |
| `internal/app/app.go` | 1333 |
| `internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go` | 1214 |
| `internal/ui/workspaces/model.go` | 1133 |
| `internal/ui/netdiag/model.go` | 995 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/registry_browser.go` | 822 |

`internal/docker/client.go` (1176 lines — the 1069 recorded earlier was stale)
was split into `exec.go`, `containers.go`, `images.go`, `networks.go`,
`volumes.go`, `registry.go`, `launch.go`, `system.go` and `parse.go`; the largest
is now 269 lines. The former `network.go` became `ports.go`, since it reports the
host's listening sockets via `ss` rather than Docker networks — the name was
free for the `docker network` family.

This interacts with the coverage work: writing several thousand statements of
tests against these files before splitting them freezes their current structure.
Decide the order deliberately. Splitting `docker` first was the cheap case — its
7.3 % coverage meant almost no tests were pinned to the old shape.

### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation —
it should run in CI even if local machines lack a toolchain.

**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.

The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
strips the path before the helper is ever called.

**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.

Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
contexts anyway.

Two smaller defects went with it:

- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
  hang indefinitely.
- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.

`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

gh pr create --base main --head fix/credential-context-isolation --title "fix: make GitLab credential contexts actually isolated" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found while planning the coverage work for `internal/credentials`. **Multi-context credential isolation has never worked.**

## The defect

All three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git credential protocol:

```
protocol=https
host=gitlab.com
path=devdesk/context/prod     ← meant to isolate contexts
username=oauth2
password=<token>
```

Git **discards the path field** unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, and it defaults to off. Every credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone.

Verified against a real credential store, before the fix:

```
approve  path=devdesk/context/default  password=TOKEN_DEFAULT
approve  path=devdesk/context/prod     password=TOKEN_PROD

$ cat .git-credentials
REDACTED      ← one entry, not two

$ git credential fill  (path=devdesk/context/default)
password=TOKEN_PROD                                ← the wrong token
```

So two contexts pointing at the same GitLab host overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate won for all of them — silently, with no error surfaced anywhere.

This affects **every helper** (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), not just `store`: git strips the path before the helper is ever invoked.

## The fix

Pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation.

Scoping it to the call is deliberate. Setting the option in the user's config would change how git resolves credentials for **every repository on their machine** — far beyond what DevDesk should be doing.

After the fix, same scenario:

```
$ cat .git-credentials
REDACTED
REDACTED
```

Each context loads its own token, and `reject` removes only the targeted entry.

⚠️ **Existing users must re-authenticate.** Credentials stored under the old path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across contexts anyway, so there is nothing meaningful to migrate.

## Two smaller defects went with it

- **`Delete` had no timeout**, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s — precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could hang indefinitely.
- **The timeout killed only the direct `git` child**, though the comment claimed it killed "le processus et tous ses enfants". The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so `Run` kept blocking anyway.

The three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built on `exec.CommandContext` + `WaitDelay`. `WaitDelay` is what actually bounds the wait on those inherited pipes, and it replaces the goroutine-and-select dance that was duplicated twice.

## Deleted `helper.go`

`HelperStorage` (137 lines) was constructed nowhere outside its own tests — `GitCredentialStorage` is what `internal/app/app.go` wires in. It was also broken:

- `detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds. A common value like `store --file=/path` became the single argv element `credential-store --file=/path` — not a command that exists.
- It hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike `GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

Deleted rather than fixed and tested.

## Testing approach

No seam. `git credential` is fully steerable through the environment, so the tests redirect `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` at a temp directory with a throwaway `store` helper. Hermetic, fast, and **nothing reaches the developer's real keychain** — which would be unacceptable in a test.

Running the real binary is what exposed the defect in the first place. A stub would have encoded the broken assumption and frozen it in place.

The 2 s timeout is covered for real by installing a credential helper that sleeps for 30 s and asserting the call returns bounded.

## Coverage

| Scope | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/credentials` | 29.5 % | **98.2 %** |
| Overall | 17.6 % | **18.2 %** |

The two uncovered lines are unreachable: a `fill` reply with no `password` field (git never produces one) and a `json.Marshal` failure on a `map[string]string`.

Phase 1 of the coverage plan is now done apart from the `ui/theme` complement (~55 stmts).

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./...` — all pass
- [x] `go test ./internal/credentials -cover` — 98.2 %
- [x] `golangci-lint run` — 0 issues
- [x] `go vet ./...` / `gofmt -l` / `go build ./...` — clean
- [x] Defect and fix both verified by hand against a real `git credential` store
- [ ] `-race` — still unrunnable locally, no C compiler on PATH (recorded as tech debt)
- [ ] Not exercised against GCM, wincred or osxkeychain specifically; the path-stripping happens in git itself, upstream of the helper, so the fix is helper-independent by construction
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

PR #8 ouverte : https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk/pull/8 — correctif + suppression de `helper.go` + couverture 29,5 % → 98,2 %. Détails à la fin.

---

## Ce qu'est un seam

Le terme vient de Michael Feathers (*Working Effectively with Legacy Code*). Un **seam** est un endroit où tu peux changer le comportement d'un programme **sans modifier le code à cet endroit**.

La métaphore est celle de la couture d'un vêtement : deux pièces sont jointes, et tu peux les séparer là sans découper le tissu.

### L'exemple du repo : `internal/docker`

Avant le découpage, chaque fonction appelait le CLI directement :

```go
func ListVolumes() ([]Volume, error) {
    output, err := exec.Command("docker", "volume", "ls", "--format", "...").Output()
    // ... parsing
}
```

L'appel à docker est **soudé** dans la fonction. Pour tester `ListVolumes`, il te faut un vrai démon Docker, avec de vrais volumes. Il n'existe aucun point où un test peut s'intercaler.

Ce qu'on a introduit dans `internal/docker/exec.go` :

```go
type dockerRunner interface {
    LookPath() error
    Run(cmd dockerCmd) ([]byte, error)
    Build(args ...string) *exec.Cmd
}

var runner dockerRunner = cliRunner{}   // ← le seam
```

`ListVolumes` appelle maintenant `dockerOutput(...)`, qui passe par `runner`. En production, `runner` est le vrai CLI. Dans un test, on le remplace par un stub qui renvoie une sortie figée. **Le code de `ListVolumes` n'a pas changé de comportement, et le test n'a rien édité** — il a juste basculé un point de décision.

Ce point de décision (ici, une variable de package) s'appelle l'**enabling point**. D'autres formes courantes : un paramètre de fonction, un champ d'interface sur un struct, une variable de fonction, un build tag.

### Pourquoi `gitlab` et `credentials` n'en avaient pas besoin

C'est le vrai enseignement des deux dernières PR. Un seam a un coût : une indirection, une interface qui n'existe que pour les tests. On n'en fabrique un que si le code n'offre **aucun point d'entrée naturel**.

| Package | Point d'entrée existant | Seam ? |
|---|---|---|
| `gitlab` | `NewClient(url, token)` — la base URL est déjà un enabling point, il suffit de la pointer sur `httptest` | non |
| `credentials` | `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` — git est **conçu** pour être piloté par l'environnement | non |
| `docker` | aucun : pas de variable d'environnement qui dise « parle à ce faux démon » et renvoie une sortie arbitraire | oui, fabriqué |

### Le piège du seam

Un stub te fait tester **ta** construction d'arguments et **ton** parsing — mais il encode aussi ton hypothèse sur ce que l'outil réel produit. Si l'hypothèse est fausse, le test passe et la production casse.

C'est exactement ce qui vient de se produire, à l'envers. Si j'avais mis un seam sur `git credential` et stubbé la réponse, le stub aurait fidèlement renvoyé le token du bon contexte — parce que c'est ce que je croyais que git faisait. Le test serait passé au vert, et le bug d'isolation serait resté. C'est en lançant le **vrai** binaire git que le comportement réel est apparu : git jette le champ `path`.

D'où la règle pratique : un seam quand la dépendance est trop coûteuse ou destructive à invoquer pour de vrai (un démon Docker, une API distante) ; le vrai outil quand il est rendable hermétique (git avec un `HOME` jetable). Ici c'était le cas, et ça a payé.

---

Sur la PR elle-même : deux défauts secondaires sont partis avec le principal — `Delete` n'avait pas de timeout alors que `Save` et `Load` en avaient un précisément pour éviter le gel du TUI, et le timeout ne tuait que le fils direct `git` alors que le commentaire prétendait le contraire (le helper survivant gardait les pipes ouverts, donc `Run` bloquait quand même). Les trois appels partagent maintenant un `runCredential` sur `exec.CommandContext` + `WaitDelay`.

À noter dans la PR : **les utilisateurs existants devront se réauthentifier**, les credentials stockés sous l'ancienne clé sans path ne correspondent plus.

Je n'ai pas mergé.

## 3. Planned features

Carried over from `todo.md`.

### 3.1 Network diagnostics

- **Port-forwarding manager** — an interactive dashboard to manage port
  redirections to the host machine.

### 3.2 Interactive security remediation

- **Auto-patch assistance** — after a Trivy scan, offer to generate a patch or an
  updated `Dockerfile` that bumps the base image version to clear critical CVEs.
- **Local SAST** — wire security linters (Gitleaks for secrets, IaC linters)
  directly into the Workspace view.

### 3.3 OCI build and cache analyser

- **Layer visualisation** — analyse a local image and show the size of each
  layer, in the spirit of `dive`. Intended approach:
  - Integrated via `google/go-containerregistry` ("daemonless", no dependency on
    the Docker daemon).
  - Talk to OCI registries directly, pulling manifests and configs without
    downloading the whole image.
  - Stream layers in memory (`tar`) to rebuild the filesystem tree.
  - Compute wasted space by detecting whiteout files (`.wh.`).
- **Cache-miss analysis** — explain why a build's cache was invalidated, e.g.
  "`package.json` changed, invalidating the cache".

### 3.4 Spontaneous dev containers

- **Configuration injection** — inject the developer's dotfiles (vim, zsh,
  aliases) when opening a terminal inside a container.
- **Hot volume mount** — mount the current working directory into a running
  container on the fly, to test a local script without rebuilding the image.

### 3.5 Resource dashboard (embedded mini-htop)

- **TUI charts** — braille-character charts showing live CPU, RAM and network I/O
  for every container in the selected project.
- **Visual alerts** — user-defined thresholds (e.g. memory saturation).

---

## 4. Existing plans

Detailed plans live in `.claude/plans/`. One is referenced directly from the old
`todo.md` and is still outstanding:

- [`platform_compatibility_improvements.md`](../.claude/plans/platform_compatibility_improvements.md)
  — Docker-layer platform portability.

### 3.6 GitHub support alongside GitLab, one active forge per context

Support GitHub as well as GitLab, with **exactly one backend active per
configuration context**. A context targets one forge; switching forge means
switching context.

Not started. The notes below are what the current code imposes on the design,
not a chosen design.

#### What is coupled to GitLab today

| Surface | Size |
|---|---|
| `internal/gitlab` + `internal/ui/gitlab/{auth,explorer}` | ~3 900 lines |
| Direct uses of `*gitlabclient.Client` outside `internal/gitlab` | 66, across 8 files |

The concrete SDK type leaks into `internal/shared/state.go:57`
(`GitLabClient *gitlabclient.Client`), so every consumer is bound to go-gitlab
rather than to a DevDesk abstraction. That field is the load-bearing change: an
interface there is what makes a second forge possible at all.

Also GitLab-shaped: `GitLabConfig` in `internal/config/config.go:41` (URL, token,
clone method, pull settings), the `gitlab-auth` / `gitlab-explorer` view names
and their `gla` / `gle` aliases in `internal/command/parser.go`, and
`shared.GitLabStats`.

#### Model mismatches to settle before coding

These are not implementation details; they decide what the abstraction can even
promise.

- **Nesting.** The explorer is a tree of groups → subgroups → projects. GitHub
  has no nested groups: an organisation holds repositories, flat. Either the
  tree degrades to two levels for GitHub, or the abstraction exposes a depth the
  backend declares.
- **Deletion.** `DeleteGroup` / `DeleteProject` implement GitLab's two-step
  permanent delete (schedule, then purge under the renamed
  `-deletion_scheduled-<id>` path). GitHub deletes immediately and has no
  equivalent, so the "permanent" checkbox is meaningless there — see also D2.
- **Dashboard counters.** `FetchDashboardStats` reads `X-Total` from five list
  endpoints. GitHub has no equivalent header for these; the counts come from the
  search API (`search/issues?q=is:open+is:pr+assignee:@me`), with different rate
  limits and semantics.
- **Vocabulary.** Group/project/merge request vs organisation/repository/pull
  request. The UI must pick per-backend labels or a neutral vocabulary; Rule 129
  applies either way.

#### Open decision: Go SDKs or the `gh` / `glab` CLIs

Worth deciding before any code is written, because it determines whether the
package needs a seam.

Arguments for the CLIs:

- Authentication is already solved, including OAuth device flow, self-hosted
  hosts and token storage. DevDesk's own credential handling could shrink — and
  it has already proven fragile (see §1.1).
- `gh api` and `glab api` are raw REST/GraphQL passthroughs, so no SDK is needed
  for coverage of endpoints the abstraction does not model.
- No SDK version churn to track for two forges.

Arguments against:

- **Per-context isolation conflicts with how these tools store auth.** Both keep
  global per-host state (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). DevDesk contexts want
  *different tokens for the same host*. Driving `gh auth switch` from the TUI
  would mutate the user's global CLI state — the exact mistake avoided in §1.1 by
  scoping `credential.useHttpPath` to the invocation. The clean route is
  `GH_TOKEN` / `GITLAB_TOKEN` per invocation, but then DevDesk still owns the
  tokens and the main benefit is gone.
- **Two more hard dependencies.** Today DevDesk needs `git`, and `docker` only
  for the features that use it. Requiring `gh` and `glab` for the core forge
  feature is a real setup-friction regression.
- **Cost per call.** A process spawn per request, against a reused HTTP
  connection today. The dashboard alone issues five calls, and the explorer
  paginates.
- **Testability regresses.** `internal/gitlab` reaches 100 % with no seam,
  because the SDK takes a base URL that an `httptest` server can stand in for.
  Shelling out would put it back in the position `internal/docker` was in, needing
  a manufactured seam — and stubbed CLI output encodes assumptions about the tool
  rather than testing against it.

**Current recommendation:** keep Go SDKs (go-gitlab, go-github) for the API
surface, and use the CLIs only as an *optional* token source — when a context has
no token, offer to read one from `gh auth token --hostname <host>` or
`glab auth status`. That takes the convenience without the coupling. Recorded as
a recommendation, not a decision.

#### Sketch of the work

1. Define a `forge` abstraction from what the code actually consumes: current
   user, namespace tree, create/delete namespace and repository, initial commit,
   dashboard counters, clone URL.
2. Replace `shared.State.GitLabClient` with that interface. This is the change
   the other 65 call sites follow from.
3. Generalise `GitLabConfig` into a per-context forge config carrying a
   `type: gitlab | github` discriminator, and migrate existing config files.
4. Implement the GitLab backend by moving the existing code behind the
   interface — behaviour-preserving, and covered by the tests added in #7.
5. Implement the GitHub backend.
6. Rename the views and commands, keeping `gla` / `gle` as aliases so muscle
   memory survives.

Steps 1–4 are worth doing on their own: they are a refactor of working code with
tests already in place, and they are what makes step 5 tractable.

---

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

D1, D3 and D6 — the byte-vs-rune lot — were fixed together; see
[§1.1](#11-fixed). The remainder is unfixed and reachable from the current code.

### D2 — The "permanent delete" checkbox is documented as locked but is not

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:35` and `:99-105`

`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent` pre-checks *Immediate deletion* and its doc
comment states the box is non-modifiable ("pré-cochée et non modifiable"). Nothing
enforces that: `space` and `enter` on the checkbox still toggle it.

A project already marked for deletion can therefore be sent through a
grace-period delete that the caller does not expect. Pinned by
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable`.

**Fix:** carry a `locked` flag on the modal and make the toggle a no-op when set,
or drop the claim from the doc comment.

### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`

`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.

Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
than a drive-by fix.

### D5 — Unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`

`internal/ui/components/creation_form.go:221-223`

After cycling the resource type, the code clamps `focusedField` down to
`maxField()`. The surrounding branch only runs when `focusedField == 0`, and
`maxField()` is never below 4, so the clamp can never fire.

Dead defensive code. Harmless, but it implies a state transition that cannot
happen and is misleading to read.

### D7 — `extractTarGz` keeps parent references in archive paths

`internal/oci/oci.go:262`

Extraction strips leading `./` and `/` but does not reject `..`, so an archive
member named `../../etc/passwd` survives as a map key containing parent
references.

**Not exploitable today.** The sole consumer, `applyTemplate` in
`internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go:1053`, turns the map into GitLab commit
actions rather than writing to disk, and the server validates the paths.

Recorded because the hazard is latent: any future caller that writes these keys
under a target directory inherits a Zip Slip. Pinned by
`TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys`.

**Fix:** reject entries whose cleaned path escapes the root, before returning
them.

### 1.1 Fixed

**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.

Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
ones.

in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered

gone.

The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).

One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.

### Test coverage

Currently **17.6 %** overall; the agreed target is 80 %, which needs roughly

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one

It deliberately records what the current code *imposes*, not a design I picked.

**The coupling, measured:**

| Surface | Size |

The concrete SDK type is in shared state, so every consumer is bound to go-gitlab rather than to a DevDesk abstraction. Recorded as an open decision with both sides, since it determines whether the package needs a seam at all.

content.text:
Entrée §3.6 ajoutée — PR #9 : https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk/pull/9 (docs uniquement).

Plutôt que d'enregistrer l'intention seule, j'ai mesuré ce que le code impose aujourd'hui :

**Le couplage, chiffré** — ~3 900 lignes dans `internal/gitlab` + `internal/ui/gitlab`, et **66 usages directs de `*gitlabclient.Client` hors du package**, répartis sur 8 fichiers.

Le point porteur : `internal/shared/state.go:57` expose `GitLabClient *gitlabclient.Client`. Le type concret du SDK est dans l'état partagé, donc tous les consommateurs sont liés à go-gitlab plutôt qu'à une abstraction DevDesk. Remplacer ce champ par une interface est ce qui rend un second forge possible — les 65 autres sites en découlent mécaniquement.

**Trois incompatibilités de modèle** consignées, parce qu'elles décident de ce que l'abstraction peut promettre, et pas seulement de comment l'écrire :

- GitHub n'a **pas de groupes imbriqués** — l'arbre groupe → sous-groupe → projet de l'explorer n'a pas d'équivalent
- GitHub supprime immédiatement ; la suppression permanente en deux temps de GitLab (`-deletion_scheduled-<id>`) n'a pas de contrepartie, ce qui rend la checkbox « permanent » sans objet côté GitHub (recoupe D2)
- `FetchDashboardStats` lit `X-Total` sur cinq endpoints ; GitHub n'a rien d'équivalent et passe par l'API search, avec d'autres limites de débit

## Sur `gh` / `glab`

J'ai consigné la question comme décision ouverte avec les deux versants, mais l'argument qui pèse le plus contre mérite d'être dit ici : **les deux CLI gardent un état d'auth global par hôte** (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`), alors que les contextes DevDesk veulent des tokens *différents pour le même hôte*. Piloter `gh auth switch` depuis le TUI muterait l'état global de l'outil de l'utilisateur — exactement la faute évitée en §1.1 en scopant `credential.useHttpPath` à l'invocation. On peut passer par `GH_TOKEN` par appel, mais alors DevDesk possède encore les tokens et le bénéfice principal disparaît.

S'y ajoutent : deux dépendances dures de plus (aujourd'hui seul `git` est requis), un spawn de processus par appel API, et une régression de testabilité — `internal/gitlab` atteint 100 % *sans* seam parce que le SDK prend une base URL qu'`httptest` peut incarner ; shell-out le remettrait dans la situation de `internal/docker`.

**Ma recommandation, consignée comme telle et non comme décision :** garder les SDK Go, et n'utiliser les CLI que comme source *optionnelle* de token — quand un contexte n'en a pas, proposer de le lire via `gh auth token --hostname <host>`. Le confort sans le couplage.

Les deux binaires sont bien présents sur ta machine (`gh` 2.89.0, `glab` 1.100.0), donc l'option est réelle et pas théorique.

Une note de séquencement dans l'entrée : les étapes 1–4 (définir l'interface, remplacer le champ d'état partagé, généraliser la config, passer GitLab derrière l'interface) valent d'être faites seules — c'est un refactor à comportement constant sur du code qui a maintenant des tests derrière lui depuis #7, et c'est ce qui rend le backend GitHub abordable.

Deux PR restent ouvertes et non mergées : **#8** (correctif isolation des credentials) et **#9** (celle-ci).

`internal/gitlab` needed no seam: every function takes a `*gitlabclient.Client`
built from a base URL, so an `httptest` server standing in for the API covers
the whole package. `Clone` is exercised against a throwaway local repository
rather than mocked, and skips when no `git` binary is on `PATH`.

`internal/credentials` needed no seam either. `git credential` is steerable
through the environment, so the tests redirect `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and
`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` at a temporary directory and run the real binary against a
throwaway `store` helper — nothing reaches the developer's keychain. Running the
real git is what surfaced the context-isolation defect recorded in §1.1; a stub
would have frozen the broken behaviour instead. The 2 s timeout is covered by
installing a credential helper that sleeps.

### Files over the 800-line ceiling

The project's own coding rules cap files at 800 lines. Seven exceed it:

| File | Lines |
|---|---|
| `internal/ui/security/model.go` | 1785 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/update.go` | 1556 |
| `internal/app/app.go` | 1333 |
| `internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go` | 1214 |
| `internal/ui/workspaces/model.go` | 1133 |
| `internal/ui/netdiag/model.go` | 995 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/registry_browser.go` | 822 |

`internal/docker/client.go` (1176 lines — the 1069 recorded earlier was stale)
was split into `exec.go`, `containers.go`, `images.go`, `networks.go`,
`volumes.go`, `registry.go`, `launch.go`, `system.go` and `parse.go`; the largest
is now 269 lines. The former `network.go` became `ports.go`, since it reports the
host's listening sockets via `ss` rather than Docker networks — the name was
free for the `docker network` family.

This interacts with the coverage work: writing several thousand statements of
tests against these files before splitting them freezes their current structure.
Decide the order deliberately. Splitting `docker` first was the cheap case — its
7.3 % coverage meant almost no tests were pinned to the old shape.

### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation —
it should run in CI even if local machines lack a toolchain.

content.text:
Aucune CI nulle part — pas de `.github/workflows/`, pas de `.gitlab-ci.yml`, aucun YAML dans le repo. Ça change ma lecture du backlog.

## Ce qui est prêt à attaquer

| Item | Taille | Bloqué ? |
|---|---|---|
| **CI GitHub Actions** | ~1 fichier | non — et c'est le seul moyen que `-race` tourne un jour |
| Phase 1 : complément `ui/theme` | ~55 stmts | non |
| Lot D5 + D7 (+ D2) | petit | non (D2 demande un arbitrage mineur) |
| Phase 2 : couverture | ~1 240 stmts | **partiellement** — `gitlab/auth` entre en collision avec §3.6 |
| §3.6 étapes 1–4 (abstraction forge) | gros | non, mais gros |
| Découpage des 7 fichiers > 800 lignes | gros | tension d'ordre avec la couverture |
| D4 (`Tab` dans `DeleteConfirmModal`) | petit | **oui** — décision qui t'appartient (mémoire musculaire) |

## Ma recommandation : la CI d'abord

Ce n'est pas dans le backlog comme item propre — c'est mentionné en passant dans « Race detector cannot run locally », qui dit *« it should run in CI »*. Or il n'y a pas de CI du tout. Donc :

- **`-race` n'a jamais tourné.** C'est la vérification la plus susceptible d'attraper une violation de la Rule 110 (modifier le modèle dans un `Cmd`), et l'app est intégralement Bubble Tea. Un runner Linux a gcc — le blocage local disparaît sans installer quoi que ce soit chez toi.
- **Les quatre PR qu'on vient de merger ne sont gardées par rien.** Build, vet, lint, tests ne tournent que quand je pense à les lancer. C'est exactement le genre d'érosion qui a laissé passer le bug d'isolation des credentials pendant si longtemps.
- C'est petit, sans dépendance sur les autres chantiers, et ça rend tout le reste plus sûr.

Deux points à décider si tu pars là-dessus : matrice ubuntu seul ou ubuntu + windows (tu développes sous Windows, et le TUI a des chemins spécifiques à la plateforme), et si on ajoute un seuil de couverture bloquant — je serais plutôt contre pour l'instant, à 18,2 % ça bloquerait tout.

Ensuite, par ordre de coût croissant : le complément `ui/theme` pour clore proprement la phase 1 (les trous sont `LoadTheme` 13,3 %, `ListThemes` 37,5 %, `OverlayBoxStyle` et `StyleTextInput` à 0 % — du chargement de fichiers, testable en tempdir), puis le lot D5/D7.

## Ce que je déconseille de commencer maintenant

La **phase 2 de couverture** inclut `gitlab/auth`, et l'étape 2 de §3.6 remplace `shared.State.GitLabClient` par une interface — ce qui touche précisément cette vue. Écrire ces tests d'abord les épinglerait sur le type concret du SDK, puis il faudrait les réécrire. Même tension que celle déjà notée pour le découpage des gros fichiers. Si tu veux avancer sur la couverture, `status`, `containers` et `dashboard` de la phase 2 sont sûrs ; `gitlab/auth` non.

gh pr create --base main --head ci/github-actions --title "ci: add a GitHub Actions workflow" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
The repository had **no CI of any kind** — no `.github/workflows/`, no `.gitlab-ci.yml`, no YAML anywhere in the tree.

Two consequences:

- Build, vet, lint and tests only ran when someone remembered to run them. The four PRs merged this session were guarded by nothing.
- **The race detector has never run.** `mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C toolchain, which the Windows development machines lack — it is recorded as tech debt in §2 with the note *"it should run in CI"*, except there was no CI. Since the whole application is Bubble Tea `Cmd`s, this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.

## Approach

Every step invokes a **mise task**, not a raw `go` command. The project deliberately has no Makefile — `mise.toml` is the task source of truth — so CI duplicating the commands would let the two drift. `mise run lint` in CI is literally `mise run lint` locally.

Two jobs on `ubuntu-latest`:

| Job | Steps |
|---|---|
| `lint` | `fmt-check`, `vet`, `lint`, `build` |
| `test` | `test`, `test-race` |

Plus `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress` so superseded pushes stop wasting runners, and `permissions: contents: read`.

## Two supporting changes

**`golangci-lint` is now pinned in `mise.toml`** alongside `go`. Without a pin, two versions disagree on what Rule 305 considers a clean run, and CI would enforce something different from what a developer sees. Pinned to 2.12.2, matching what is installed locally.

**New `fmt-check` task.** This one is a real gap I hit while writing the workflow: `mise run fmt` runs `go fmt ./...`, which *rewrites* files and therefore can never fail. It is usable as a fix, not as a gate — so `mise run check`, described as the pre-commit checklist, silently reformats instead of reporting. `fmt-check` prints the offending files and exits non-zero.

I did **not** change `tasks.check` to depend on `fmt-check`: that would alter the local pre-commit workflow, which is a separate call for you to make. Worth deciding, since `check` currently cannot fail on formatting.

## Verified locally

- `mise run fmt-check` on a clean tree — passes
- `mise run fmt-check` with a deliberately malformed file — exits 1 and names the file (a check that can only pass is worth nothing, so this direction was tested too)
- `mise run vet`, `mise run build`, `mise run lint` (0 issues), `mise run test` (all packages ok)
- `mise` resolves `golangci-lint 2.12.2`, and `mise run lint` works through it

## What I could not verify

- **`mise run test-race`** — this is precisely the check that cannot run on this machine. Its first execution will be on this PR. If it surfaces a real race, that is the workflow doing its job on day one, and I will fix what it finds before merging.
- Two tests skip on Windows and will execute for the first time on Linux: `TestLaunchOptionsCache_FilePermissions` and the permission branch of `TestFileStorage`. Both assert `0600`; `launch_options.go:76` and `storage.go:160` both write `0600`, so they should pass.

## Test plan

- [x] Every CI step run locally except `test-race`
- [x] `fmt-check` verified in both directions
- [ ] `test-race` — first run is this PR
- [ ] Workflow triggering confirmed (branches reach GitHub through the Entire mirror)
EOF

input.new_string:
### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.

**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
run reported no data race across all 17 packages.

That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
tests actually execute, and coverage is 18.2 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
paths — most of the view layer — remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so
this is an argument for the coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.

Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.
